SD-4 puts every paper in the mailings since the previous meeting on the agenda (f:agenda-papers), and a meeting's hours are fixed (ax:hours), so publishing a later part early takes review time from the first. Ease of review then also gives a reason to keep later parts out of the mailings, so inf:pa-tell-apart does not tell the two explanations apart.
fix: Narrower subject: compare later parts kept out of every form of publication with later parts made available outside the mailings, such as drafts, implementations, or talks, which put nothing on the agenda and which ease of review gives no reason to withhold.

problem: The withholding it attributes to the model is predicted only for design-bound authors (inf:pa-design-bound, l:first-part-smallest). A result-seeking author in the settled pattern gains nothing from it, and the record does not show which type an author is (f:no-interest-statement). Large proposals by result-seeking authors that publish later parts early would then count against the stated prediction, though the model never predicts withholding for them.
fix: Scope stated once: "For design-bound authors, the model predicts that later parts already drafted or implemented stay out of the mailings until the first is adopted," and say that the test applies only to large proposals whose authors are design-bound, which the record does not identify.

problem: "gives no reason to leave out later parts that already exist" is unsupported. A longer paper takes more time to review (ax:review-cost), so an author taking small steps to lower risk has a reason to keep the first paper to the first step, leaving existing later parts out of it. Both explanations then predict existing later parts left out of the first paper, and inf:fp-tell-apart does not tell them apart.
fix: Narrower subject: compare whether existing later parts were kept out of every publication before the first part's poll, or published separately, which the lower-risk explanation gives no reason to avoid.

problem: As in inf:pa-tell-apart, leaving out existing later parts is predicted only for design-bound authors, since inf:fp-small and inf:fp-seldom rest on l:settled-design-bound, and the record does not show an author's type. First papers by result-seeking authors that set out later parts would count against a prediction the model does not make for them.
fix: Scope stated once: "For design-bound authors, the model predicts that first papers seldom set out later parts even when those parts already exist," with the test limited to them.

problem: "Novelty measures how well understood a topic is" is an added premise with no axiom or fact behind it: a novel topic can be well understood by the experts working on it, and an old one poorly understood. The test's control for how well a topic is understood then rests on an unstated assumption.
fix: Add the premise once as a stated assumption of the test, or replace novelty with a measure a cited item ties to understanding, such as implementation experience before adoption (l:implementation-informs).

problem: Check the proof does not state: SD-4 says that "if the specification subgroups have already reviewed an entire new working draft paper with changes applied," plenary approves the changes in that form, and "an editing committee is not needed since it has already been verified that changes were applied correctly." In that case the changes first come together in the wording room, not at the editor's merge, and no pre-ballot editing committee verifies them.
fix: Add a Fact quoting both whole sentences (SD-4, "Working draft handling"), and scope the first sentence to papers approved as change papers. The absence of an SD-4 step checking whether designs work together stands.

problem: Check the proof does not state: SD-4 says a presentation "requires that the presenter be qualified to answer detailed questions about design constraints in the problem domain, design alternatives considered and how they worked out, and so forth at a level that the group as a whole does not already know." Reviewers of a first part can therefore ask the presenter what later parts will need of it, which limits how far the first part is adopted before reviewers can weigh those needs.
fix: Add a Fact quoting the whole sentence word for word (SD-4, "Proposals and papers"), and state in this proposition and its child on what reviewers can foresee that reviewers can ask the presenter about later parts, though ax:first-review still keeps them from studying those parts in detail until they are presented.

problem: "a cost absent before" is false as written. ax:rework puts a cost on "changing a design after work is built on it" whether or not a poll has passed, and authors and sponsors often build wording and implementations before the first direction poll. What the axioms add after a favorable poll is more work built on the design, not a new kind of cost, so the claim that a like rival loses support from incumbency itself is unsupported, and inf:rp-tell-apart's "Passing the direction poll alone" inherits the gap.
fix: "a cost that grows with the work built on the design after the favorable poll (ax:rework)"; in inf:rp-tell-apart, predict the loss as that work grows, and compare only polls between which the incumbent's content and review time did not change while work built on it, such as implementations or dependent papers, did.

problem: The comparison holds for opponents who together can cast a third of the Favor-plus-Against votes, not for each opponent. An opponent whose Against vote leaves the result unchanged (l:objector-effect) pays the standing and reasons cost of p:against-costs-more for nothing by voting Against early, while waiting costs nothing until they seek removal. p:first-part then sizes the design-bound author's first part against Against votes that foreseeing opponents who are not pivotal do better not casting.
fix: Narrow the subject: "So opponents who foresee the rest, and whose Against votes together can reach a third of the Favor-plus-Against votes, do better voting Against the first part than waiting to seek its removal after adoption"; in p:first-part, say "against the Against votes that opponents who foresee the rest do better casting".

problem: The extra Favor votes a large proposal draws from its own authors come from having two or more authors, each of whom values adoption of the proposals they support (ax:prefer) whoever pays them. The definitions bundle the number of authors with sponsorship, and d:large lets each author have a different sponsor, so a limit on how many participants one sponsor pays may vote need not bind at all. The step from the authors' votes to "the votes of participants sponsors pay" is unsupported, and c:lever-sponsor-limit's prediction rests on it.
fix: Narrow the subject to proposals whose authors one sponsor pays in greater number than the limit, and predict smaller margins for them compared with proposals that have the same number of authors paid by separate sponsors.

problem: "only while that vote brings it more than that cost" is false as written. A participant also brings papers, review, and presentations, and a proposal the sponsor values is considered only with an invested presenter (f:present-required, f:invested), so a sponsor can do better paying for a participant whose vote alone is worth less than the cost. l:settled-sponsor and the Theorem's sponsor clause inherit the vote-only test.
fix: "So, apart from any paper, presentation, or review the participant brings, the sponsor does better paying for one more only while that vote brings it more than that cost."

problem: ax:support says an Against voter "cannot rule out" less ready support, with no condition on whether the colleague learns of the vote, so the axioms do not give that anonymity lowers the risk. The step needs a premise, and in a small room a colleague can often tell who voted Against from the count and the discussion.
fix: Add a premise to ax:support, for example "A colleague can support a participant less readily for a vote only as far as the colleague can tell how the participant voted," and narrow c:lever-anonymous to rooms where the count does not reveal who voted Against.

problem: Technical views can change with the work a participant does, and a move to another sponsor changes that work (ax:attention: what a participant learns can change their vote). Participants also choose sponsors whose technical direction they share. So a change in votes after a move does not separate a sponsor's interests from technical views, and the comparison does not tell the two apart.
fix: Narrow the comparison to moves that leave the participant's work on the topic unchanged, such as a change of sponsor through an acquisition, and say that votes changing after such a move favor the model.

problem: "Reviewing in parts is as easy when later parts already drafted or implemented are in the mailings" is false as written. An unfinished draft of later parts adds reading, and no participant can study every paper (ax:review-cost, ax:attention), so an author who splits a design for ease of review also has reason to hold back drafts that are not ready. Both explanations then predict such drafts staying out of the mailings, and inf:pa-tell-apart's test fails.
fix: Change the test to whether the first paper states that later parts exist and what they will require of it, a statement that costs reviewers little: ease of review gives no reason to omit it, while the model predicts its omission (f:no-parts-step).

problem: "gives no reason to leave out later parts that already exist in drafts, implementations, or talks" is false as written. Later parts that exist only in drafts, implementations, or talks are provisional and may change once the first part is used (ax:unknown), and lowering risk is a reason to keep provisional designs out of a paper that asks for a poll. Omitting existing parts then fits both explanations, and inf:fp-tell-apart's test does not separate them.
fix: Narrow the test to later parts the author already treated as settled, such as parts the author's own implementation ships or the author proposed elsewhere, or to whether the first paper mentions that later parts exist at all.

problem: The comparison is unsupported. A sponsor stops paying once a participant is worth less to it than the cost (l:settled-sponsor), a large proposal faces more meetings than a small one (p:large-position), and a small proposal's author expects review within one meeting (d:small), so small proposals can more often finish before costs mount. The model fixes no rate for either kind, so it does not say which stops more often without a negative poll.
fix: Narrow the prediction to stops per meeting spent waiting behind priority work, comparing self-funded and sponsored authors of papers of similar length.

problem: Reflection also predicts a difference by who pays. A sponsor weighs a proposal before paying for it (ax:prefer, l:settled-sponsor), so a sponsored proposal has been reflected on before its first paper, and fewer sponsored proposals are dropped on reflection later. More stops by self-funded authors then fit both explanations.
fix: Compare the same authors' proposals before and after they gain or lose a sponsor, on papers of similar length, so reflection before submission is held fixed.

problem: A flaw found later also costs its authors and their sponsors, through rework of what they built (ax:rework) and possibly standing (inf:omit-exposure). The sentence sets the authors' gain at the poll against a later cost that falls only on users, and l:thm-costs-gains repeats the contrast, which overstates how far the timing separates authors from the cost of a flaw.
fix: "Authors get the adoption they value at the poll, while a flaw that implementation and use have not yet exposed costs them only later and in part, and can fall on any user of the feature."

problem: Check not stated: the design room can direct the author to set out what later parts will require of the first part, and an author who declines should defend that with new information and harms the proposal's chances (f:direction-implement), while the chair may take any poll, including one asking to see the rest first (f:chair-polls). This limits the effect the sentence describes wherever the room suspects a partial design.
fix: Add: "A design room can direct the author to state what later parts need of the first, though only reviewers who foresee the rest have reason to ask." *[from f:direction-implement, f:chair-polls]*

problem: Check not stated: SD-4 asks whoever notices a potential problem to "File the issue or write the paper, or otherwise make sure such a follow-up happens," and to make sure the feature's authors know of it (SD-4, "How to report a potential technical concern, at any level of severity"). This limits how often an objection's argument stays unwritten, which the proposition and the Theorem's "finds unwritten objections kept only in memory" describe.
fix: Add the quoted step as a Fact, and add to the proposition: "SD-4 asks whoever reports a concern to file an issue or write a paper, though no rule requires it."

problem: Check not stated: ISO says meetings "should, as a general rule, be organized in locations where entry restrictions or other constraints do not significantly limit the ability of participants to attend," and has hosts provide invitation letters on request and make reasonable efforts on accessibility needs (ISO/IEC Directives Part 1, 5.3.1). These limit the cost of taking part, which the proposition treats as the gate on who votes.
fix: Add the quoted sentence as a Fact under f:iso-meetings, and begin the proposition: "Fees are barred, meeting places should not significantly limit attendance, and everyone in a subgroup's room has one vote, yet ..."

problem: d:stake defines a stake in one poll, but a user who takes part can affect every poll they attend and gains standing and knowledge of how the committee applies its rules (ax:learning, d:standing), so taking part can bring more than "their stake" in any one poll. As written, l:user-take-part and the Theorem's user clause understate what taking part can bring.
fix: "Taking part can bring the user no more than the sum of their stakes in the polls they take part in, with the standing and procedural knowledge taking part builds"; use that sum as "their own stake" in l:settled-user and the Theorem.

problem: Neither poll results nor paper lengths show stakes, so the named evidence cannot hold "similar stakes" fixed, and a longer paper often covers a larger topic in which more participants have stakes, which draws more votes. The prediction as stated cannot be checked against the evidence it names.
fix: Name an observable that holds stakes close, for example successive revisions of one proposal polled in the same room, or narrow the prediction to such revisions.

problem: "the other explanation predicts few such requests wherever removals are few" is false as written. A removal request reflects its requester's view, not need, so many requests with few removals fit the view that adopted designs rarely need removal as well as the model.
fix: Compare the margins of failed removal polls instead: requests drawing more Favor than Against votes but no more than twice as many favor the model's hurdle, while requests failing with more Against than Favor votes fit the other explanation (d:follows-norm).

problem: "those the chair's summary shows were answered favor the other explanation" is false as written. The model predicts papers omit objections whether or not they were answered in discussion, since a written answer costs time and makes the objection easier to raise again (inf:wa-cost). Omitted objections that were answered fit both explanations; only those not answered favor the model.
fix: "those the chair's summary shows were not answered favor the model, and those it shows were answered fit both."

problem: The model also predicts defects where no one voted Against: a proposal costing more to read than most stakes in it is voted on mainly by those with large stakes and can advance with no change (p:light-review), so defects no one raised can be more common in features forwarded with no Against votes. The model's own results point both ways, so they do not fix the sign of the predicted difference.
fix: Add the number of votes cast to the matching in inf:de-tell-apart, and state the prediction among features forwarded with similar numbers of votes cast.

problem: The rule asks voters of every position, so Favor would also bear a reasons cost. A regular who now votes Favor on a doubted proposal because Favor costs "no time for reasons" (l:doubt-options, inf:favor-cost) would then do better not voting, so the model also predicts fewer Favor votes, which bears on whether proposals meet the 2:1 norm. The stated effect is incomplete.
fix: "...Neutral and Favor would bear the reasons cost Against now bears, while not voting would bear none. The model predicts fewer Neutral votes, fewer Favor votes on doubted proposals, and more participants not voting."

problem: Declaring consensus on a count above 2:1 can itself depart from SD-4, whose definition requires "the absence of sustained opposition to substantial issues by any important part of the concerned interests" (f:consensus-def), and a national body's experts united Against can be such a part. Nothing in the axioms lets the chair rule out that declaring over that opposition puts their post at risk, and p:chair-threshold names a cost of declaring that the ranking leaves out. So the ranking, l:dchair-call, and the Theorem's "Chairs follow the 2:1 norm" hold only where the chair judges no such opposition.
fix: Narrow the subject: "On a count above 2:1 after discussion, with Neutral votes short of a majority and no opposition the chair judges sustained by an important part of the concerned interests, ...", and state that scope once in d:follows-norm.

problem: The list leaves out that national bodies, as SC22's P-members, appoint and reappoint the convenor, and that the convenor's own national body confirms the appointment (f:convenor-term). That move is the route of the convenor's post risk in ax:post-risk and l:convenor-depart, yet l:nb-other-moves and l:thm-pattern test the national body's choices without it.
fix: Add "vote in SC22 on the convenor's appointment, and confirm it when the convenor is its own expert," and add to l:nb-other-moves that this vote goes with whichever ballot vote the body casts.

problem: "WG21 considers its comments whatever its vote" leaves out that ISO directs effort at negative votes: "Every attempt shall be made to resolve negative votes" (f:respond-comments, f:pmember-consensus), which the proposition cites. Comments behind a No can draw more effort than the same comments behind a Yes, so the table's case and the Theorem's "whose comments fare the same under any vote" rest on SD-4's statement against an ISO rule pointing the other way.
fix: Add "though ISO asks that every attempt be made to resolve negative votes," and state in the table caption that the case assumes the body expects that rule to make no difference to how its comments fare.

problem: Check not stated: INCITS lets an absent voting member vote by correspondence on an issue to be acted on at a meeting, "provided it is received by the Chair prior to the point when the issue is brought to a vote" (INCITS Organization, Policies and Procedures, 5.2). This limits how much presence at a meeting adds to an organization's weight, which the proposition's question about paid participants turns on.
fix: Add the 5.2 sentence to f:incits-one-vote, and add to the proposition "and lets an absent voting member vote by correspondence before an issue is put to a vote."

problem: The INCITS rule the step cites, one voting membership per organization, governs votes of INCITS bodies. For a position formed during a plenary, INCITS lets the delegation decide "by consensus of the U.S. caucus as determined by the HoD" (f:incits-caucus), which sets no limit per organization, so an organization with many delegates present can weigh more there. c:lever-nb-more varies the cost of forming positions during meetings, so its prediction of less weight for how many participants each side has present is unsupported for exactly those positions.
fix: Narrow the subject to positions a national body sets before the meeting through votes of its member organizations, as INCITS's TAG does, or add a cited fact that a body counts its caucus during a meeting by organization.

problem: A failed final draft does not remove the feature: it goes back to SC22, which may resubmit a modified draft, publish a Technical Specification, or cancel the project (f:failed-fdis), and a resubmitted draft can keep the feature. Valuing the feature's removal at least as much as the rest of the document therefore does not make a failed document worth as much as one that passes with the feature, and l:nb-no, l:settled-nb, and the Theorem's national body clause rest on this step.
fix: State the condition as the body's value of a failed ballot: "for a body that values what a failed ballot leads to, given SC22's choices, at least as much as the document passing with that feature," and use that condition in l:nb-no, l:settled-nb, and the Theorem.

problem: The cost explanation also predicts positions concentrated on contested proposals, since a body forms a position only where that is worth its members' time (inf:nb-cost), and a proposal drawing Against votes in subgroups is likelier to touch interests it values. Both explanations predict more positions where there are Against votes, so the comparison does not tell them apart.
fix: Vary the cost instead: compare national bodies, or meetings, where forming a position costs more or less, such as bodies whose experts attend in person against those taking part only by email lists; the model predicts more positions where the cost is lower, and agreement predicts no such difference.
